exact_claim: Strasbourg, July 1518: a dancing epidemic lasting into late August/September
Began with Frau Troffea on about 14 July, dancing alone without music
She danced for 4-6 days; her husband begged her to stop
Within days, more than thirty people were dancing
notes: ACCEPTED WORDING (user rule 2026-11-21: plain-English rounding of this sourced fact; claim-decisions.md): 'Within days, more than thirty.' (S1: 'the chronicles say' in line 3 covers the Troffea story and its spread)

exact_claim: One chronicle counted 400 afflicted within a month
Frau Troffea was taken to the shrine of St. Vitus (Saverne)
Physicians: 'a natural disease, which comes from overheated blood'; prescribed dancing it out
Council converted guild halls, built stages in the horse and grain markets, hired musicians (drums, pipes, horns) and strong men to hold dancers up
It backfired; more people joined
Stages pulled down; public music and dancing banned until September; at weddings only strings, no tambourines or drums
Worst cases sent by wagon to St. Vitus shrine; red shoes, crosses, holy water
Deaths ('as many as 15 a day')
notes: Only as: later chronicles claimed it; the city's records of the time don't mention deaths

exact_claim: Cause unknown; one leading interpretation is stress-induced mass psychogenic illness; the ergot theory is contested
More than ten dancing outbreaks along the Rhine and Moselle since 1374
Paracelsus claimed Troffea danced to annoy her husband
notes: Humour beat; flag as his opinion

exact_claim: She danced for hours until she collapsed exhausted; next morning she was up again on swollen feet and dancing
source_1: Pennant-Rea, 'The Dancing Plague of 1518', Public Domain Review, 10 Jul 2018 (read 2026-11-21): 'she continued for hours, until the sky turned black and she collapsed in a twitching heap of exhaustion'; 'she was up again on her swollen feet and dancing'
notes: The essay narrates the Paracelsus/chronicle account; say 'according to the chronicles' once for the Troffea story. No blood on her feet in any source read: don't show or say it.

exact_claim: By the third day a growing crowd of all kinds of people (hawkers, porters, beggars, pilgrims, priests, nuns) was watching her
source_1: Pennant-Rea, 'The Dancing Plague of 1518', Public Domain Review, 10 Jul 2018 (read 2026-11-21): 'By the third day, people of a great and growing variety' were watching (hawkers, porters, beggars, pilgrims, priests, nuns)

exact_claim: After four to six days the frightened authorities intervened and sent her by wagon to the shrine of St Vitus at Saverne, where it was believed she might be cured
source_1: Pennant-Rea, 'The Dancing Plague of 1518', Public Domain Review, 10 Jul 2018 (read 2026-11-21): 'The mania possessed Frau Troffea for between four and six days, at which point the frightened authorities intervened, sending her in a wagon thirty miles away to Saverne'; 'There she might be cured at the shrine of Vitus, the saint who it was believed had cursed her'; later: 'the shrine of Saint Vitus, where Frau Troffea had been cured'
dispute_status: the essay says both 'might be cured' and 'had been cured'
notes: Say she was taken there to be cured; whether she was cured is not firm: hedge ('the chronicles say' / 'it seems'), never 'there she finally stopped' as fact.

exact_claim: The clergy held the plague to be the work of a vengeful Saint Vitus; at the shrine the afflicted were given small crosses and red shoes, sprinkled with holy water and marked with crosses of consecrated oil
source_1: Pennant-Rea, 'The Dancing Plague of 1518', Public Domain Review, 10 Jul 2018 (read 2026-11-21): 'the work of a vengeful Saint Vitus'; 'They put small crosses in their hands and red shoes on their feet'; 'On the soles and tops of these shoes, they sprinkled holy water and painted crosses of consecrated oil'
